note: The register of work for the FETCHING (kartaan-com/Kartaan-AutoSync).
Kartaan-ERP has one of these and a tools/status.py that turns it into a
board. This repository has no such tool yet, so nothing generates anything
from this file. It is written by hand and read by a person.
WHY IT EXISTS. This repository was split out of the ERP on 2026-08-31 (D148)
and the four register entries covering it -- `autosync`, `shared-place`,
`github-actions`, `extension` -- came out with it and were not written down
again anywhere. The only way to know what was built here was to read all of
it. That is what this closes.
THE FOUR ENTRIES ARE SPLIT INTO SEVENTEEN, and the reader adds more. `autosync` was one entry covering
the report list, what is owed, the run log, landing, the day board, both
doors, the recipes, the runner and the alarms -- nine separate pieces with
one review record between them. Split, because a review of the day board
says nothing about the alarms.
ONE OWNER PER FILE. `files` is what the piece IS, and no two pieces list the
same path -- two owners means two answers to 'has it been reviewed' about the
same bytes. `also_touches` is what a piece has to CHANGE without owning.
`rests_on` follows the imports, not the story.
THE THREE HONEST COLUMNS. `state` answers three different questions that this
project has previously let collapse into one word:
built          the code exists and its own checks pass
reviewed       somebody who did not write it has read it, and when
run_for_real   it has done its actual job, against real accounts and real
credentials, and produced a real file
NOT ONE PIECE IN THIS REPOSITORY HAS EVER RUN FOR REAL. The nightly job has
never been installed in a seller's GitHub account, never held a real token,
never fetched a report, never landed a file and never written a row. Every
`run_for_real` below is false, and each says what WAS done instead so that
'checked' is never read as 'working'.
TWO PIECES HAVE TOUCHED REALITY WITHOUT RUNNING, and it is worth saying
exactly how far:
the extension  was loaded unpacked into his own Chrome on 2026-08-27 and
driven READ-ONLY against his real Meesho panel and his real
Flipkart dashboard. Nothing was clicked, submitted or
downloaded. It found seven faults no check could. It has
never fetched a file.
the day board  and the report list were measured BY HAND against his real
Drive files -- 96 real Meesho payment files, 494 real Meesho
rows -- by scripts in the ERP's audit folder. This code did
not do that reading.
THE CHECKS. 2,300 Python checks and 400 JavaScript checks pass, 2026-09-02,
AND A GATE NOW MAKES THEM RUN -- see `the-gate`. Before 2026-09-02 they were
green because a session remembered to, and 0 of the first 11 commits carried
any record that a person read the diff.
They are checks, not a run. Every door in this package has its transport
handed in, which is what lets them pass with no account, no token and no
internet -- and is also exactly why passing them proves nothing about a real
night.
SEVEN PIECES HAVE BEEN PROVED BY BREAKING THEM ON PURPOSE -- the seven the
reader is made of, and no others. `tools/prove_checks.py` lives in the ERP and there is still no copy here
(open item 10 in the ERP's memory), so that one piece was done by hand: eight
eighty-eight faults put back one at a time; eighty-six caught by a NAMED check
and two by a second guard, proved by removing both. TEN OF THE EIGHTY-EIGHT
FOUND GAPS IN THE CHECKS RATHER THAN IN THE CODE -- including a check helper
that hid a fault, a proving pass that called a crash a survivor, and a rule
whose own check could not fail for it. That is the argument for doing this to
everything else. **Every other piece here has checks nobody has
ever watched fail.**
THE READER IS STARTED, 2026-09-02. His go-ahead: Meesho, Flipkart and Amazon.
`reading-a-file` is the first piece of it and the floor the rest stands on. It
is also the first piece in this repository ever PROVED by breaking it on
purpose -- eight faults put back one at a time, eight caught, no survivors,
and two of the eight found real gaps in the checks rather than in the code.
READING A SPREADSHEET IS DONE TOO, 2026-09-02, and it had to be: all 67
Flipkart order files and all 186 payments files are .xlsx, not text.
WHAT A SALE IS, DONE TOO, 2026-09-02, with its columns and its name read out
of the ERP's own source and compared rather than retyped.
THE COLUMN MAPS ARE DONE TOO, 2026-09-02. All three platforms' orders files
read against his real ones: 121 real sales, not one unreadable row.
THE SHEET DOOR IS BUILT, 2026-09-02. His 121 real sales go in, and the same
files again write nothing at all -- not even a call. **But NO REAL CELL HAS
EVER BEEN WRITTEN: no seller's sheet exists, and nothing yet creates one
(D137 says Kartaan must, because `drive.file` cannot reach a sheet the seller
made by hand).**
WHAT STARTS A READ IS BUILT TOO, 2026-09-02.
STILL TO COME: nothing yet REMEMBERS which files have been read across runs --
`between_runs.Between` has no field for it, and adding one bumps its SHAPE;
whatever CREATES the seller's sheet; the PAYMENTS files,
which is where Flipkart's money lives since its orders file has none; and
D152's new columns, which cannot be added here until the ERP adds them too --

THE HOLE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE PRODUCT: THE READER IS ONE PIECE OLD. Files are
downloaded and landed in the seller's Drive, and NOTHING YET TURNS THEM INTO
NUMBERS -- `reading-a-file` turns a file into rows and stops there, on purpose.
Until the pieces above it exist, every one of Kartaan's twenty tabs still shows

Nothing replaces them yet.

items.name: What a report IS
items.what: One list, and it is the whole design (D100). Every report the fetching knows about -- which platform, which door, what it is called, how it is asked for, whether it can be asked for again for a past day. Adding a report is one entry here and nothing else. The single best thing in the working reference was that `config.js` was the only place a report was described; this is that, checked.

Also holds D110's asking for a day by hand: the same code the nightly run uses, never a second program, and everything refused is in the log BEFORE anything is fetched.

items.name: The run that starts itself, with nobody present
items.what: D111, D113 and D120. Every piece of auto-sync existed and nothing joined them; this is the joining. The job wakes on a schedule in the seller's own GitHub Actions and `clock.py` refuses the ticks that are not due -- the hour is a FLOOR, not an appointment, because GitHub's own docs say a scheduled run can be delayed and a missed appointment is a day lost (D108). FIVE things survive a run and live in the seller's own Drive -- the fifth, added 2026-09-02, is WHICH FILES HAVE ALREADY BEEN READ, and it is a LIST OF FILE IDS and never a date: a file that fails and arrives days later is simply not in the list and is read, where a high-water date would skip it for ever and say nothing (D110). A MISSING record and a DAMAGED one are not the same thing: missing is a first night, damaged STOPS the run, because read as empty it asks Amazon again for every report it is already building. `start.py` DECIDES NOTHING -- it reads the secrets and opens the connections; every rule is in `nightly.py` where it is checked. `transport.py` is the only file in the package that opens a connection.

findings.what: D113: nothing carries the seller's chosen hour to the job. Superseded in part by D114 -- the job now READS the hour off the seller's own business record -- but the workflow has never been installed anywhere, so the path is unexercised.

**THE RECORD'S SHAPE WENT FROM 1 TO 2** to carry `files_read`. An existing shape-1 record now REFUSES and stops the run -- deliberate, and the reason the number exists. Costless only because no record exists: checked, not assumed. The day a seller has one, this costs them a night.
findings.proved_by: `between_runs_checks.py` -- 'a record written before this field existed refuses rather than reading as a first night', red when SHAPE is left at 1.

state.instead: 336 checks pass, all with the transport handed in. THE WORKFLOW HAS NEVER RUN, in this repository or any seller's. `start.py` -- the one file that reads the GitHub Actions Secrets and opens the real connections -- HAS NO CHECKS FILE OF ITS OWN and has never been executed. That is the single largest untested surface here.

items.name: Putting a file in the seller's own Drive
items.what: D100 and D131. The raw file lands untouched, before anything reads it. `drive.py` decides, `drive_door.py` does -- transport handed in, so every line is checked with no account and no internet. A write refused for storage says so, so a full Drive is reported as 'your Google Drive is full, today's files were not saved' rather than as the platform giving nothing (D108, D131). The run holds `drive.file` only, which never sees a file it did not create -- reading the seller's Drive quota would cost the same annual security assessment as full control of it, and that was refused.

findings.what: **THE FOLDER WAS READ ONE PAGE DEEP AND THAT WAS TAKEN AS THE WHOLE FOLDER.** All three listings called Drive's files.list with no pageSize, no pageToken and no following of nextPageToken. His flipkart folder holds ~800 files and meesho ~470, so most of the folder was never seen -- and nothing said so. **AND THE `fields` MASK IS WHY IT COULD NOT BE NOTICED:** Google's own documentation on partial responses says a mask of `files(id,name)` returns ONLY that, so `nextPageToken` never arrived at all. The listing looked complete because the one thing that would have contradicted it had been filtered out of the reply. **THREE OF THIS FILE'S OWN CHECKS PINNED THE FAULT** by asserting the mask was exactly `files(id,name)`. Fixed: one pager for all three listings, pageSize asked for explicitly at Drive's documented maximum of 1000, nextPageToken followed to the end, a repeated page marker refused rather than looped, and **a listing Drive itself calls `incompleteSearch` refused rather than believed.** Every parameter read off Google's live reference on 2026-09-02 (Golden Rule 1).
findings.proved_by: `drive_door_checks.py` -- 'A FOLDER OF 850 FILES COMES BACK AS 850, NOT AS ONE PAGE', 'A LISTING DRIVE ITSELF CALLS INCOMPLETE REFUSES RATHER THAN BEING BELIEVED' and 'A SECOND FOLDER OF THE SAME NAME ON A LATER PAGE IS STILL SEEN'. Nine faults were put back one at a time and all nine went red on a named check.

state.instead: 112 checks pass against a stand-in transport. NOT ONE BYTE HAS EVER BEEN UPLOADED to a real Google Drive by this code. The Google app is still in Testing, so any refresh token it did hold would die after seven days.

items.name: What the run writes into the seller's own database

Every moment goes in as TEXT, because a timestamp would be read as UTC and shown five and a half hours wrong. `True` is an `int` in Python, so booleans are asked about first. The chosen hour is READ and never written.

items.name: Turning a platform's file into rows
items.what: The floor the whole reader stands on: take the bytes a platform handed over and say what rows are in them, or say why a row could not be read. It knows nothing about sales, settlements, SKUs or money, and it never hands back a number -- turning "0" into 0 is a decision about a FIELD, and D119 says the money rules are written once, somewhere else. **Written against his real files, not a description of them.** Four faults those files actually have: Amazon ends every line with CARRIAGE-RETURN CARRIAGE-RETURN NEWLINE, so the plain way of counting lines reports 93 orders where there are 46; all three Amazon files are named `.csv` and all three are TAB-separated, so what separates the columns is read out of the file and never off its name; Meesho's comma file quotes every field while Amazon's tab files contain not one quote character, so quoting is off for tab and on for comma; and **a row of the wrong width is named and kept, never dropped** -- the reference read its files with on_bad_lines='skip', which loses the row AND says nothing. **AND A HEADER IS NOT ALWAYS ON LINE 1 (added 2026-09-02):** a real Meesho returns file opens with a seven-line title block -- a blank line, the panel's name, the supplier's own details, a timestamp -- with the column names on LINE 8. Read from line 1 that file names no columns at all and the whole returns stream was unreadable. The separator is decided from the header's own line too, since a title block two cells wide says nothing about the columns below it.

findings.what: A check named 'a quote character in a tab file does not swallow the columns after it' COULD NOT FAIL for that fault. Its sample put the quote in the MIDDLE of a field (`9" Bangle`), and a quote that is not the first character never opens a quoted field -- so the file read identically whether the rule was there or not. Exactly the shape of the log-line-name check this project already shipped: named for the fault, passing through it.
findings.found: 2026-09-02, by putting the fault back and watching nothing go red
findings.proved_by: autosync/table_checks.py -- the sample now starts a field with a quote. Taking `quoting=csv.QUOTE_NONE` back out turns two checks red.

Only Meesho orders and Amazon read as text, so without this Flipkart cannot be read at all. Nothing is installed to do it and nothing needs to be: an `.xlsx` is a zip of XML, so `zipfile` and `xml.etree` are enough. **It hands back the same `table.Table` a text file does**, so everything above cannot tell which arrived and the rules about refused rows and missing columns stay written once.

GST)`, at columns 18 and 26, holding different figures, beside 41 good ones. `table.py` refused the whole FILE on a duplicate name, which would have made Meesho payments permanently unreadable over one column.

findings.proved_by: It now separates CRASHED from SURVIVED and says the breakage proved nothing.

state.instead: 66 checks, and they read HIS REAL SPREADSHEETS -- his Flipkart orders (39 columns, 63 rows), his Flipkart payments (74 columns, 77 rows, header on row 2, 16 sheets) and his Meesho payments (43 columns, 83 rows). **Proved by breaking it on purpose: twelve faults put back one at a time, twelve caught, no survivors** -- and two of those twelve found gaps in the checks rather than in the code. The spreadsheets the checks build are built by hand out of zip and XML, because one made by the same code that reads it would agree with itself about anything. Never run inside a real run, and no independent reviewer has read it.

items.name: What a sale IS, and the row it becomes
items.what: **Sales do not go in the database. They go in a GOOGLE SHEET (D126)** -- a Sheet is for what the pipeline writes and Kartaan only reads; the database is for what Kartaan's own clicks change. His own numbers decided it: one document per sale means a screen opening reads thirty thousand of them, most of a day's free allowance, at his current 83 orders a day. **The columns are not invented here -- they belong to the ERP**, and are written out again only because Python cannot import JavaScript. A sale is named `platform::orderId::sku` from the sale itself, which is what makes the same file arriving twice change nothing. Nothing here writes anything anywhere: putting a row in a sheet is a door, and it is not built.

findings.what: **THE CHECK'S FIRST VERSION GAVE A CONFIDENT, SPECIFIC, WRONG ANSWER ABOUT REAL DATA.** Reading the ERP's column list with a plain quote-matching pattern, it reported that the two sides DISAGREED and named two columns called things like `s shelf it would come out different...`. Those were sentences out of the COMMENTS beside the list -- the ERP explains `taking` as "the whole of D51's replay safety", and that apostrophe opened a string as far as the pattern was concerned, swallowing `took` and inventing two columns that do not exist. The lists were identical all along.
findings.found: 2026-09-02, on the first run of the checks
findings.proved_by: Comments are stripped before anything is read, at all three read sites. Dropping a real column, swapping two, or renaming a charge each turns the comparison red -- proved by doing all three.

state.instead: 60 checks. **The important ones read the ERP's own source and compare, name by name and in order** -- `sheet-store.js` for the columns, `charges.js` for the charge ids, `orders.js` for how a sale is named and what states it can be in. Neither list is typed out in the check. They REFUSE rather than skip when the ERP cannot be found, proved by pointing them at nothing. **Proved by breaking it on purpose: thirteen faults put back one at a time, thirteen caught, no survivors.** No sale has ever been written to a real sheet -- there is no sheet door yet.

items.name: Which of a platform's own columns is the SKU, the quantity, the money
items.what: **The only file that knows what Meesho, Flipkart and Amazon call things.** Above it a sale is a sale; below it a file is rows. One word for one thing, said once, so a seller comparing two platforms compares like with like -- and a renamed column is one entry changed here and nothing else. Every column name was read off HIS OWN FILES, not off a description of them. **A moved column stops the whole file ONCE, by name, checked against the header before a row is read** -- per row it would produce 63 identical complaints and bury the one fact that matters. **A row that cannot be read is refused by name and the rest are read.** **And a date is never guessed at**: all three orders files lead with the year, and a shape it does not know stops that row rather than dating it wrong -- because Amazon's settlement file writes day-first, where 1 September read backwards becomes 9 January.

findings.what: **FLIPKART'S ORDERS FILE HAS NO MONEY IN IT AT ALL.** Thirty-nine columns and not one is an amount -- no price, no GMV, no settlement. Counted on his real file, not assumed. So a Flipkart sale is read with its money BLANK, which means what it should: nobody has worked this out yet. The figure arrives later from the payments file as a second statement about the same sale. **This is why blank and nought had to be different things before this file could be written at all.**
findings.proved_by: The money is never among the columns a file cannot do without; making it one turns a check red, and Flipkart would never read again.

findings.what: **EVERY ONE OF HIS 63 REAL FLIPKART SKUs IS WRAPPED** as `"""SKU:DJ 14 Bahubali"""`. Left wrapped it matches no product he has. The wrapper is the file format's, not the seller's.
findings.proved_by: The wrapper comes off and NOTHING ELSE does -- not case, not spacing inside the name. The register already carries the fault that rule exists for: 'a tidy-up map sat inside an identity lookup, so 17 of 39 mapped SKUs could never match'. Adding any tidying turns a check red.

findings.what: **THE PLATFORM'S OWN WORD FOR WHAT HAPPENED HAS NOWHERE TO GO.** Counted on his real August Meesho files: 209 SHIPPED, **42 CANCELLED**, 37 READY_TO_SHIP, 5 HOLD, 4 DELIVERED. Kartaan's ledger has no column for it, deliberately -- `sheet-store.js` says so in as many words. Putting it in `notes` would overwrite the seller's own typing (D136); dropping cancelled rows would mean a cancellation never corrects yesterday's sale. **Adding a column changes the pinned contract on both sides, and that is HIS decision, not one to be made in passing.**

state.instead: 74 checks. **It reads all three of his real orders files: 12 real Meesho sales, 63 real Flipkart, 46 real Amazon -- 121 sales, and NOT ONE unreadable row.** The rows that must NOT read are built by hand, because his real files are clean and a check that only ever read them would say nothing about what happens when one is not. **Proved by breaking it on purpose: fourteen faults put back one at a time, fourteen caught, no survivors.** Not one of those sales has ever reached a sheet -- there is no sheet door yet.

items.name: What goes into the seller's sales ledger, and what is left alone
items.what: **Where D150 and D152 live.** The ledger exists so one row explains one order without opening Kartaan. A row is one LINE of an order, not one order, so a return lands on the exact item that came back. **Rule 1: each report writes only the columns it knows about** -- a payments file landing three weeks late must not wipe a delivery date it knows nothing about. **Rule 2: where two claim the same column the newest file wins, by the FILE'S OWN DATA DATE**, so the order of fetching decides nothing. **Rule 3: two files of the same date disagreeing KEEP what is there and REPORT it** -- never a silent pick. **And saying nothing is not saying "nothing": a blank never overwrites a figure already there.** A sheet whose columns somebody dragged about is refused; a row with no id, or a sale on two rows, is named and neither written to nor added again.

findings.what: **A REPORT THAT KNOWS A COLUMN BUT SAYS NOTHING FOR IT WOULD HAVE BLANKED WHAT WAS ALREADY THERE.** Rule 1 keeps a report out of columns it knows nothing about; this was the same fault one level down -- a payments file DOES know about the settlement, but the row it holds for one sale may carry no figure, and writing that blank wipes a real settlement written last week.
findings.found: 2026-09-02, by a check named for rule 1 going red
findings.proved_by: autosync/ledger_checks.py -- 'A BLANK NEVER OVERWRITES A FIGURE THAT IS ALREADY THERE'.

findings.what: **A SALE'S NAME WAS PARSED BACK OUT OF A SENTENCE MEANT FOR A PERSON** -- `why.split()[1]` on "the sale X is already on row 2" returns the word "sale". So the rule that stops a doubled name being written to did nothing at all.
findings.proved_by: `Unreadable` carries `name`; removing BOTH guards turns 'A SALE ON TWO ROWS IS REPORTED and NEITHER is written to' red.

findings.what: **A SALE THE SHEET HELD TWICE WAS APPENDED AGAIN, making three rows.** Taking it out of what the sheet holds -- so neither row is written to -- made it look like a sale never seen before.
findings.found: 2026-09-02, by the check named for exactly that
findings.proved_by: A doubled name is skipped both ways and reported once.

findings.what: **RULE 2 CANNOT BE ENFORCED ACROSS RUNS with the columns that exist.** The ledger's 28 columns hold no record of WHICH FILE last wrote each value, so tomorrow's run cannot tell whether a cell came from an older or newer file than the one it holds. Harmless for ordinary nights -- a new file is newer by construction. **NOT harmless for a by-hand backfill (D110)**, where a deliberately old file is fetched after newer ones have written. Recency IS exact within one run. Fixing it needs a column that is not in D152's list.

**TWO FILES OF ONE REPORT AND ONE DATE SILENTLY OVERWROTE EACH OTHER**, and D150 rule 3 says a same-date disagreement is KEPT and REPORTED. The rule was applied only when the reports differed -- but a day fetched again lands as a NEW FILE of the same report and the same date (D110), which `whats_new` correctly calls new. **And the first half of the fix was not enough: the sort still tied on the report, so a stable sort kept whatever order the files were handed over in and the order of FETCHING decided which figure stood** -- precisely what rule 2 exists to stop.
findings.found: 2026-09-02, by the review of this repository (REVIEW.md findings 1 and 2)
findings.proved_by: autosync/ledger_checks.py -- 'RULE 3: TWO FILES OF ONE REPORT AND ONE DATE ARE TWO STATEMENTS', 'RULE 3: the order they were handed over in decides nothing', and 'but TWO ROWS OF ONE FILE are still one statement'.

state.instead: 57 checks, run against HIS REAL FILES: **121 real sales planned into an empty ledger, and the same three files again change nothing.** **Proved by breaking it on purpose: thirteen faults put back one at a time, twelve caught by a NAMED check and the thirteenth by a second guard, proved by removing both.** Three of the thirteen found gaps in the checks rather than in the code.

items.name: Writing the sales ledger
items.what: The doing half. **The transport is handed in**, so every line is checked with no Google and no internet -- and the stand-in RECORDS every call, so what is checked is the request that would really go out. **Every call is the one Kartaan already makes**, read off the ERP's own `sheet-store.js` rather than worked out again: one GET for the whole ledger, `:append` with RAW and INSERT_ROWS to add, `values:batchUpdate` with RAW to change. **It needs no permission the seller has not already given (D137)** -- `drive.file` is accepted by the Sheets API, which is why KARTAAN MUST HAVE CREATED THE SHEET and a pasted id is refused in words. **Changes go first and additions last**, because a plan's row numbers describe the sheet as it was read. It never removes a row, never writes to row 1, and makes NO call at all on a night with nothing to write.

findings.what: **THE HEADER'S OWN CALL WAS UNCHECKED.** `write_the_header` and `carry_out` send the same two options, so a fault put into the header's call -- RAW turned into USER_ENTERED, INSERT_ROWS into OVERWRITE -- went unnoticed by every check in the file. OVERWRITE on the header would write column names over a seller's first sale.
findings.found: 2026-09-02, by the proving pass, twice over
findings.proved_by: Three checks now read the header's own call; both breakages turn them red.

state.instead: 49 checks against a stand-in that records every request. **His 121 real sales were written through it end to end, and the same files again made NO write call at all.** Six checks pin the calls against the ERP's own `sheet-store.js` through the door, refusing rather than skipping when it is not there. **Proved by breaking it on purpose: ten faults, ten caught.** NOT ONE REAL CELL HAS EVER BEEN WRITTEN TO A REAL GOOGLE SHEET -- no sheet exists, and nothing yet creates one.

items.name: What starts a read
items.what: **His rule, and the word 'solely' is his: a read starts on what NEW file is in the Drive folder, and on nothing else.** Never whether a fetch succeeded or failed -- D148 says why: one platform having a bad night must not cost the day's numbers. **It is enforced STRUCTURALLY:** the decision is handed the folder and what was already read, and nothing else, and the module cannot even import anything that knows whether a fetch worked. **Identity is Drive's own id, NEVER the name** -- `landing.py` names a file for the day its data is about, so a day fetched again lands under the same name, and keyed by name that correction would never be read (D110 exists because somebody naming a day by hand usually knows what arrived was wrong). **An empty file is new, is not data, is reported by name, and is NOT marked as read** -- so tomorrow's real file for that day is still new.

findings.what: **A THIRD CHECK WRITTEN WITH A DEAD `if False` ON THE END** -- green by construction. Third one on this project, all three mine.
findings.proved_by: Replaced by two that really ask it; the empty-file breakage turns them red.

findings.what: **A CHECK THAT SCANNED THE SOURCE FOR FORBIDDEN WORDS WAS THE WRONG CHECK.** It read the docstring too, so the sentence explaining that a day fetched again must still be read made it go red about the word 'fetch'. Prose is not code.
findings.proved_by: It now checks what the file can REACH -- that `runlog`, `board`, `schedule`, `reports`, `runner` and `nightly` are not importable here, so the rule cannot be broken by somebody passing the wrong thing.

findings.what: **NOTHING REMEMBERED WHICH FILES HAD BEEN READ ACROSS RUNS.** What survives a run is `between_runs.Between`, and it had no field for it, so the list was rebuilt from nothing every night and every file in the folder looked new. FIXED 2026-09-02 by one field, `files_read`, and the SHAPE bump that goes with it. **The bump was checked before it was made, not assumed:** no `autosync-state.json` exists anywhere in the seller's Drive, and the only two scheduled runs this repository has ever had both stopped at 'no platform is connected' before any of this code ran.
findings.proved_by: `between_runs_checks.py` -- 'THE FOURTH FILE, ARRIVING AFTER THE FIFTH, IS READ ON THE NEXT NIGHT' and 'and the four already read are not read a second time'. Both go red when the list is not written, not read back, or replaced by a high-water mark.

findings.what: **WHAT HAS BEEN READ GREW FOR EVER.** `now_read` never dropped an id, and once the list survived the night it really did grow -- roughly 7,000 file ids a year at his volume, in a file in the seller's own Drive. **FIXED 2026-09-02, HIS DECISION, HIS WORDS: 'cap on folder'.** An id is let go of ONLY when its file has gone from the folder, never after so many days -- because a landed file is never removed, so a day-cap would let go of ids for files still sitting there, and each one read again would put its old figures back over newer ones. The list is now a mirror of the folder: never longer than it, and it shrinks the night he tidies Drive.
findings.proved_by: `whats_new_checks.py` -- 'A FILE THAT HAS GONE FROM THE FOLDER IS LET GO OF', 'A FILE FROM MONTHS AGO IS STILL REMEMBERED WHILE IT IS STILL IN THE FOLDER' and 'AN EMPTY FOLDER LISTING LETS GO OF NOTHING AT ALL'. All three go red when the cap is made a day-count, or when an empty listing is read as a tidied folder.

findings.what: **THE CAP RESTS ON THE FOLDER LISTING BEING THE WHOLE FOLDER, AND IT WAS NOT.** `drive_door` called Drive's files.list with no paging at all and took the first page as the whole folder. His flipkart folder holds ~800 files and meesho ~470. A short listing looks exactly like a tidied folder from inside `whats_new`, so the cap would have let go of ids for files still sitting there -- and, far worse, the reader would never have SEEN those files to read them at all. **FIXED 2026-09-02 in `the-drive-door`.**
findings.proved_by: `drive_door_checks.py` -- 'A FOLDER OF 850 FILES COMES BACK AS 850, NOT AS ONE PAGE'. Red the moment the listing stops following nextPageToken.

state.instead: 42 checks. **Proved by breaking it on purpose: eight faults, seven caught by a NAMED check; the eighth was a no-op breakage -- the behaviour is protected structurally, confirmed by running it. It has never chosen a file in a real folder: nothing calls it yet.**

items.name: The gate, so the checks are not run because somebody remembered to
items.what: **2,206 checks passed here and NOTHING MADE THEM RUN**, and 0 of the first 11 commits carry any record that a person read the diff (D156). Follows Kartaan-Server's gate (cf648d9) rather than inventing a shape. **Every rule is in `tools/gate.py`, never in the hook** -- a rule written in a git hook is a rule nothing can test, and the ERP's hook once PRINTED that it had tagged a commit and never did, undetected across three commits. It refuses a commit that carries a credential, leaves the register disagreeing with disk, has any checks file red, or has nothing recording that somebody READ it. **The tag goes on in `commit-msg` because a pre-commit hook structurally cannot rewrite a message**, and the review record is consumed so it cannot be reused. `.github/workflows/pm_check.yml` is the half `--no-verify` cannot walk past.

findings.what: **THE JAVASCRIPT CHECKS WOULD NOT HAVE RUN.** The Server's gate sweeps only Python because it has only Python. Copied as-is, this gate would have reported green while 400 checks over the extension -- the half that runs in the seller's own Chrome -- never ran. The same shape as the Server's own gate not sweeping its `tools/`, which it found by reading what it printed.
findings.proved_by: tools/gate_checks.py -- 'THE JAVASCRIPT ONES ARE FOUND TOO'; and the register sweeps .js as well.

findings.what: **THE WORKFLOW WOULD HAVE RUN IN EVERY SELLER'S GITHUB ACCOUNT.** D36 copies this repository into each one, and the workflow cannot pass there: its checks are pinned against two PRIVATE repositories a seller has no token for. Every seller would carry a permanent red cross for a rule about how Kartaan is developed. Guarded to `kartaan-com` only, with the cost of the guard stated in the file: a seller's copy has no gate on GitHub, which is right because nobody develops there.
findings.proved_by: tools/gate_checks.py -- 'IT RUNS ONLY IN KARTAAN'S OWN ORGANISATION'.

state.instead: 88 checks on the gate's own rules, including one that reads all THREE copies of `NOT_CODE` off disk -- Python, the commit-msg hook, and the workflow -- and holds them to each other. The workflow has never run: nothing has been pushed.
